title: Eating from the forest: Food forest movement reaps harvest across Maryland landscape
summary: Lincoln Smith's 10-acre food forest is next to a gas station and a church off a highway in Bowie, a reclaimed cornfield that is part of growing number of food forests across the U.S. that are growing food in rewilded urban spaces.
content:
by Rosanne Skirble, Maryland Matters October 31, 2025

by Rosanne Skirble, Maryland Matters October 31, 2025

Lincoln Smith’s food forest is next to a gas station and a church off a highway in Bowie.

Smith says his mission as the director of Forested is to rewild this former cornfield, stripped in the course of Maryland’s agricultural history of its trees, its soil depleted and biodiversity drained by industrialized single-crop food production.

“We’re trying to restore [the] forest and produce food for people in a forested agroecosystem,” he said.

When he rented 10 acres from the neighboring church in 2012, the first thing Smith did was to take note of what was already there. Luck would have it that a stand of mature native trees formed a natural border, and beneath their canopy were wild black raspberry bushes and persimmon trees, whose seeds were spread into the field by wildlife that ate the fruit.

Now, on this fall day, Smith and crew harvest those persimmons, plus other native and nonnative fruits and berries from the bushes, gardens and trees that cover the landscape.

“We have over 100 species that we’ve planted, as well as many species that we didn’t plant, that are wild and that we’ve allowed to come in and grow here,” Smith said.

“We grow in layers,” he said. “We have big trees together with understory-size trees and shrubs and vines and patches of vegetables, and native flowers to support beneficial insects and habitat for the birds that eat those insects.”

Smith says that as the forest grows, people come, just to walk around, pick its fruits and attend workshops and other events like the twice-yearly Forest Feast, a multicourse, forest-to-table chef meal.

“[This fall] we had baklava made from butternuts, chestnuts and hazelnuts and dried persimmons. We had acorn crostini topped with berry jam, imitation crab cake made from a beautiful lion’s mane mushroom together with our hot peppers and herbs, and sweet potatoes seasoned with some of our nuts,” he said.

Forested is part of a growing food forest network in the U.S. In Maryland, that includes the Maryland Forest Service and Queen Anne’s County Edible Forest Trail in Centreville, Long Creek Nursery in Frederick, the Reed Center for Ecosystem Reintegration in Middletown, and a food forest behind a Brunswick food bank.

Add to that list the Takoma Park Elementary School, and two sections on the Takoma Park/Silver Spring Montgomery College campus. Those projects are led by Miles Amoore, co-founder of the nonprofit Community Food Forest Collective, and Tierney Acosta, a Montgomery College horticulture student, who leads the college permaculture club.

Over the weekend, both were giving tours at the Community Food Forest Collective Fall Food Festival. The three-quarter-acre college site at the corner of a busy intersection includes broad sections filled with herbs, vegetables, wildflowers, berry bushes, grape vines, hops and nut trees.

Work at the site began in 2023 with 450 cubic yards of leaf moss, wood chips and compost. Amoore says the earth responded with early signs of an emerging diverse ecosystem.

“It turned grass into soil and insects and bees and fungal life came back almost overnight,” he said.

The rest of the food forest, with the exception of a mature stand of oaks and holly trees already there, went in by design, with the help of nearly 500 volunteers, many recruited by  Acosta from her peers at the college, students and friends.

“We’ve planted several thousand plants and over 100 different species found within our watershed,” she said. “Now it is alive and thriving, not only for humans, but for wildlife, and the amazing thing about planting this way in multiple layers is that it really feeds itself, and is really resilient.”

Acosta says the food forest also plants an opportunity.

“It is really just a fun place to connect with your community,” she said. “[This] is a time when we are so polarized, we really wanted a place where you can just come and be who you are.”

Whether that means attending any of the day’s workshops that range from how to make acorn flour, pickle cucumbers, brew Ethiopian coffee, use fig leaves in a range of Turkish dishes or pasta making with freshly picked garden herbs, Amoore says, the food forest can also sow seeds of change.

“It’s about bringing people in relationship to the land and with each other. We want thriving spaces that are hubs for education, gatherings, celebration, ritual and joy,” he said.

Amoore’s vision is to expand food forests into communities and schools across the region.

“These hubs can have a ripple effect by reconnecting people to the land, to each other and to the source of food,” he said.

Smith, trained in landscape design, says, the food forest mimics the structure and function of a natural forest. Unlike the cornfield, its diverse biosystem helps protect it, and keeps it thriving. A diverse population of predatory insects helps control pests.

It’s here that Smith brings clients, including private landowners and municipal officials, to show them how to adapt his ideas to their properties.

“We need to have healthy, thriving ecosystems full of biodiversity and wildlife habitat and water filtration, building soil and sequestering carbon. All that needs to happen in our production lands,” Smith said, adding that each new food forest is a step in that direction.

Smith works with a small paid staff as well as dedicated volunteers who take on multiple tasks year-round, from pruning to planting. On this day, volunteer Jenn Mott is harvesting the last of the hot peppers, among the many chores she’s taken on since January, when she discovered Forested.

She says here she can step outside of her daily work routine into the restorative powers of the forest.

“Mother Nature takes care of us,” she said. “With just a tiny bit of effort, she rewards us and sustains us with so much abundance, not just with food, but also, emotionally and spiritually.”

Arman Milanian agrees. The University of Maryland graduate student is among the longest-serving volunteers, coming regularly for over a decade.

Today he is helping supervise homeschooled children and their parents in removing vines and picking a large haul of sweet potatoes. He says the space pulls him in.

“[It’s] the amount of birds, the amount of insects, the amount of flowers, the amount of food. Those are gifts from Nature,” he said. “[We’ve] invited Nature in, and Nature provides.”
